2000 CanLII 21310 (CA IRB)
1 A99-00575/6/7 
 The following are my decisions and reasons for decision in the claims of XXXXXXX and XXX XXX. I find XXXX and XXXXXXXXX to be C onvention refugees and found XXXXXXXXX not to be a Convention refugee. XXXX, XXXX and XXXXXXXXX are the minor children of XXXXXXXXXXand the XXXXXXXXXX. The claimants are all stateless Palestinians. XXXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXX were born in and resided in Syria until the family's departure from Syria to pursue studies and work opportunities related to their studies in France and the United States. On the 27th of June 2000, I determined that XXX and his wife XXXXXXXXXX were Convention refug ees for the reasons I set out from the bench on that date, which were subsequently issued in writing on the 24th of August 2000. The present reasons should be read in conjunction with those other reasons. At the time, I indicated that I could reach no determination in the claims of the minor claimants, XXXX, XXXX and XXXX without firs t considering additional evidence. This evidence, contained in Exhibits A4 and D15, is now before me, as are counsel's able submissions in regard to these claims. On the basis of their parents' evidence, summarized in my reasons in those claims, I am able to find that these three minor claimants, on the basis of the membership in their family as Palestinians and as well on the basis of their tender ages, in view of the provisions of a number of international instruments addressing the needs and rights of children, face more than a mere possibility of persecution in Syria. 
2000 CanLII 21310 (CA IRB)
2 A99-00575/6/7 
 The key questions that remained at the conclusion of the hearing in which I found their parents to be Convention refugees are in connection with the status of XXX, age 3, as a U.S. citizen and the possible status of XXXX and XXXX as citizens of France. XXXX and XXXXXXXXX were born in France. Th ere is evidence before me that suggests the possibility of their having access to French citizenship in accord with the provisions of the French Civil Code at article 19-1, as cited in Response to Information Request FRA35077, which is Exhibit A5. Evidence before me in Exhibits A2 and D15, the latter, an affidavit counsel has submitted along with her submissions, suggests that while French citizenship may be acquired by operation of the Jus Sanguinus and Jus Soli. The Jus Soli provisions are not absolute. Even in the case of the children of stateless people born in France, the mere fact of birth on French soil is not sufficient, apparently, to assure acquisition of French citizenship. The potential applicant's residence in France is a key factor in determining the access to the acquisition of French citizenship. XXXX and XXXX are not residents of France and have been outside France for five years. Moreover, it appears that their parents' recognition as Convention refugees in Canada may also be an obstacle in the path of their potential recognition as French citizens. Finally, a French consular official in Ottawa has recognized that the cases of XXXX and XXXX are particularly complex. These various factors lead me to find that the access to French citizenship for XXXX and XXXX is not sufficiently established to allow me to conclude that they can reasonably be expected to be recognized by France as citizens. In that I have found that these two young claimants have a well-founded fear of persecution in Syria, and likewise have found insufficient evidence which would allow me to find that they 
2000 CanLII 21310 (CA IRB)
3 A99-00575/6/7 
 could avail themselves of the protection of France, I conclude that XXX and XXXXX XXX are Convention refugees. XXXXXXXXX is three years old. XXXX is a citizen of the United States. As such, she benefits from the protection of the United States. There is insufficient evidence before me to rebut the presumption that the United States is able to provide XXXX with protection. It is within my specialized knowledge, again from hearing numerous such claims, that United States authorities have ample agencies and provisions in law and regulation to afford XXXX the protection she requires if she were to be returned there. I find that XXXXXXXXX does not face more than a mere possibility of persecution in the United States, where she is a citizen, and thus find that she is not a Convention refugee. I would add by way of some general post-decision observations, in particular for the benefit of XXX's parents, that while counsel has submitted that XXXX's return to the United States would create a forced separa tion from her parents and has argued that such could be construed to be persecutory, I have no evidence before me indicating that XXX's parents have approached U.S. officials to discuss what possibilities may in fact exist for them to live with XXXX in the United States should XXXX be returned to the United States. I would add as well, and again with no bearing on my decision, that while I have no mandate to act on what amounts to a family reunification request, provisions do exist within the Immigration Act to address the issue of XXX remaining with her family in

 Canada, her parents and siblings having been determined to be Convention refugees in Canada. CONCLUSION For the reasons given above, having considered all the evidence before me, I find that XXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXX are Convention refugees and that XXXXXXXXX is not a Convention refugee. This concludes these reasons. These reasons will be issued in both official languages of Canada. "XXXXXXXXXXXXXX" XXXXXXXXXXXXXX Dated at Ottawa this 23rd day of January 2001.
